questions.q: Mama Ngozi's son wants to "write a program" for her shop's totals. Which part of that work is the real core of programming?
questions.explain: A computer does exactly what it is told and never fills a gap with common sense. Most of programming is deciding those exact steps: what goes in, in what order, and what to do in every case. Typing them is the smaller part.
options: Typing the code as fast as possible
Turning a job she does with judgement into steps exact enough for a machine with no judgement
Choosing the most popular programming language

questions.q: What is the difference between an algorithm and a program?
questions.explain: "Start at 0 and add price × quantity for each item" is an algorithm. You could follow it on paper. Written in JavaScript, Python or Go, it becomes a program. One algorithm can become many programs.
options: An algorithm is a short program; a program is a long algorithm
An algorithm always runs faster than a program
An algorithm is the method, written in any language or none; a program is that method written in a programming language
There is none: the two words mean exactly the same thing

questions.q: Which of these steps could not appear in an algorithm?
questions.explain: An algorithm's steps must be precise: anyone following them must get the same result. "If it seems fair" depends on judgement, so two people would do different things. The rule must say exactly when delivery is added.
options: Multiply the price by the quantity
If the amount paid is less than the total, report what is still owed
Add delivery if it seems fair
Subtract the discount from the subtotal

questions.q: A set of steps says: "1. Set the counter to 1. 2. Add 1 to the counter. 3. Go back to step 2." Why is this not a correct algorithm?
questions.explain: Algorithms may repeat, but they must be finite: every repetition needs a condition that eventually stops it. The savings exercise stops when the savings reach the goal. This one has no stopping rule, so it has no output.
options: It never finishes, and an algorithm must stop and produce its output
It uses numbers instead of words

questions.q: A currency app takes an amount in naira and today's exchange rate, and shows the amount in dollars. What is the processing?
questions.explain: The naira amount and the rate are the input. The number shown on the screen is the output. The calculation that turns one into the other is the processing.
options: The amount in dollars on the screen
Dividing the naira amount by the exchange rate

questions.q: In the IPO model, what is the input of a web server?
questions.explain: A request comes in (input), the server finds or changes data (processing), and a response goes out (output). Every backend you will write sits in the middle of that.
options: The HTTP response it sends back
The processor of the computer it runs on

questions.q: The laundry charges ₦500 per shirt and ₦800 per trousers, with ₦1,000 off from 10 pieces. Which of these is an input to the bill program?
questions.explain: The prices and the discount are fixed rules written on the board. What changes from one customer to the next is how many shirts and trousers they bring, so those are the inputs. The amount to pay is the output.
options: How many shirts the customer brought

questions.q: In the problem-solving loop, which step comes right before "implement"?
questions.explain: The order is understand, break down, inputs, outputs, design steps, implement, test, improve. You write the algorithm in plain language first, then turn those steps into code.

questions.q: Why should you work out the expected answer before running a program?
questions.explain: The first laundry program printed ₦6,200 with no complaint. Only someone who had already worked out ₦5,200 could see it was wrong. Looking at an output and thinking "seems fine" is how bugs survive.
options: Because the computer refuses to run code without it
Because a logic error prints no message: you can only see a wrong output if you already know the right one
So you do not need to test afterwards

questions.q: The rule is "orders of ₦20,000 or more get free delivery". Which set of test inputs is best for finding a boundary bug?
questions.explain: Boundary bugs, like writing > where the rule says "or more", only show up at the value where the answer switches. Test just below, exactly on, and just above it. Values far away give the same answer for both the right and the wrong code.

questions.q: What is source code?
questions.explain: You write source code, such as a .js file. An engine like V8 translates it into machine code, which is what the processor actually runs.
options: The numbers the processor runs directly
The program as text, written by a person in a programming language
The list of inputs a program needs

questions.q: Your JavaScript file calls console.log, but you never wrote a function by that name. Where does it come from?
questions.explain: A runtime is the engine plus the extra tools a program needs: printing, files, network, timers. console.log is one of those tools.
options: From the runtime (Node.js or the browser), which gives your code tools like printing
From the source code of the file above it

questions.q: A shop's board says: "Buy 3 or more, get 10% off." You are at step 1 of the loop, understand. Which question is most worth asking the owner?
questions.explain: The rule can be read two ways, and each reading gives different bills. No amount of careful coding fixes an unclear rule. Asking takes seconds; guessing wrong makes every bill wrong.
options: Which programming language should I use?
Does it mean 3 of the same item, or 3 items in total?
How many customers come each day?
What colour should the receipt be?

questions.q: A delivery fee of "500" comes from a web form. Why can 3600 + deliveryFee give the wrong total?
questions.explain: 3600 + "500" gives the text "3600500". Input from a keyboard or form is text until you convert it, for example with Number(deliveryFee). Never use an input before you have checked what it really is.
options: Because 500 is too large to add
Because form input arrives as text, and + glues text together instead of adding
Because JavaScript cannot add numbers from the internet
Because the fee must be added before the total exists

questions.q: A receipt program prints Change: ₦-400 and no error. What went wrong?
questions.explain: The arithmetic was right; the design was incomplete. The fix is a decision: if the amount paid is less than the total, print what is still owed. Most real bugs are missing cases like this, and none of them produce an error message.
options: A syntax error: the minus sign is not allowed
A runtime error: the program crashed
A missing case: nobody decided what to do when the customer pays less than the total

questions.q: A checkout rule says: "Members get 10% off. Delivery is free when the price after discount is ₦15,000 or more." Which order of steps is correct?
questions.explain: Delivery depends on the discounted price, so the discount must be worked out first. Deciding delivery on the price before discount gives free delivery to some members who should pay for it.
options: Decide delivery, then apply the discount, then add them up
Apply the discount, then decide delivery on the discounted price, then add them up
Add delivery, then apply the discount to everything

questions.q: Which input value do people forget to think about most often, and is worth a test in almost every program?
questions.explain: Zero is the smallest normal input and the easiest to forget. In the receipt, a quantity of 0 is fine; a customer with 0 items might not be. Either way, you only know if you asked.
options: Zero or nothing: no items, ₦0, an empty order

questions.q: The receipt program runs for two different customers. Between the two runs, what should change?
questions.explain: The processing is written once and works for every customer; only the input changes, and so the output changes with it. That is what makes a program worth writing.

questions.q: Look at the chain problem → algorithm → source code → machine code → output. Which arrows are the programmer's job?
questions.explain: You think of the steps and write them as source code. The engine translates it into machine code and the processor carries it out; that software was written by someone else. That is why most of programming happens in the first two arrows.
options: Problem → algorithm and algorithm → source code
All of them: the programmer writes the machine code by hand

questions.q: All the laundry tests pass. Then the owner adds a rule: "20 pieces or more: ₦2,500 off". What does the problem-solving loop tell you to do?
questions.explain: A new rule is a new problem to understand. It adds a new boundary, so it needs new tests just below and on it. The old tests stay, because the 10-piece rule still applies to 10 to 19 pieces.
options: Nothing, the old tests already pass
Go back to understand with the new rule, update the steps, and add boundary tests at 19 and 20 pieces
Delete the old tests, because the rules changed

questions.q: Which input should a program check most carefully before using it?
questions.explain: Anything that comes from outside the program, such as a keyboard, a form or a network request, can be mistyped or even sent on purpose to cause harm. Values the program set or calculated itself are under your control.
options: A price the program itself calculated a line earlier
A quantity a user typed into a web form
A fixed discount written in the code

questions.q: This is meant to print the cost of 4 tins of sardines at ₦800 each. What does it print?
questions.explain: The code says +, so the computer adds: 800 + 4 is 804. It has no idea you meant multiply. This is a logic error: no message, just a wrong answer that only someone who expected 3,200 would notice.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Multiplication happens before addition. The first line adds 3,000 to 0; the second adds 1,000 to 3,000. total ends at 4,000.

questions.q: What does this receipt print?
questions.explain: Rice is 2 × 2,500 = 5,000 and oil is 1 × 3,000 = 3,000, so the total is 8,000. The change is 10,000 − 8,000 = 2,000.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: + works from left to right. "Total: ₦" + items is text, so adding delivery to it glues 500 on the end. Brackets fix it: "Total: ₦" + (items + delivery) adds the numbers first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The change was calculated on line 3, while total was still 0. Setting total afterwards does not go back and change change. The program runs top to bottom, so the steps must be in the right order.

questions.q: The rule is "10 pieces or more: ₦1,000 off". What does this print?
questions.explain: pieces > 10 means "more than 10", and 10 is not more than 10, so the discount stays 0. The rule says "10 or more", which is pieces >= 10. A boundary test at exactly 10 is what catches this.

questions.q: What does this loop print?
questions.explain: The loop starts at 1, runs while shirts <= 3, and adds 1 after each round: 1, 2, 3. In "shirts cost ₦" + shirts * 500 the multiplication happens first, then the number is glued to the text.
options:
1 shirts cost ₦500
2 shirts cost ₦1000
3 shirts cost ₦1500

0 shirts cost ₦0
1 shirts cost ₦500
2 shirts cost ₦1000

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 4,000 is not greater than or equal to 4,500, so the else block runs. It subtracts the other way round, total - amountPaid, which gives 500.

questions.q: Members get 10% off, and delivery (₦1,500) is free from ₦15,000 after discount. What does this print for a customer who is not a member?
questions.explain: isMember is false, so there is no discount and afterDiscount stays 16,000. That is ₦15,000 or more, so delivery is free. A member would pay 14,400 + 0 = 14,400, which is below 15,000, so they would pay 15,900 including delivery.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: After 3 weeks the savings are 18,000, still below 20,000, so the loop runs again. After 4 weeks they are 24,000 and the loop stops. The loop only checks the condition before each round, so it can overshoot the goal.

questions.q: The fee came from a form as text. What does this print?
questions.explain: With text on one side, + glues: "5000250". Number(fee) turns the text into the number 250 first, so the second line adds properly.

questions.q: Fares: children under 5 ride free; otherwise ₦300 up to 5 km and ₦500 beyond. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both inputs sit exactly on a boundary. 5 < 5 is false, so a 5-year-old is not free. 5 <= 5 is true, so a 5 km trip costs ₦300.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Instructions run top to bottom. 10 − 3 is 7, which is printed. Then 7 + 5 is 12. Each line starts from whatever value stock has at that moment.

questions.q: This should print the cost of 6 tins of sardines at ₦800 each, Total: 4800, but it prints the wrong number. Fix the processing line.
questions.explain: The cost is price times quantity, so the operator must be *. With + the computer adds and prints 806, without any warning.

questions.q: The input is written for you. Add the processing and output so the program prints the total and the change: Total: ₦7500 and then Change: ₦2500.
questions.explain: The change is the amount paid minus the total. "Change: ₦" + change glues the text and the number into one line.

questions.q: This prints a negative change when the customer pays too little. Change it so that, in that case, it prints Still to pay: ₦700 instead. Keep printing the change when the customer pays enough.
questions.explain: Paying too little is a separate case, so it needs its own branch. if handles "paid enough"; else handles everything else and subtracts the other way round.

questions.q: The rule is "10 pieces or more: ₦1,000 off". For 10 pieces this program prints To pay: ₦5000. Fix the condition so it prints To pay: ₦4000.
questions.explain: "10 or more" is >=. > means "more than", which leaves out exactly 10: the classic boundary bug.

questions.q: This program works out the change before the total is known, so it prints Change: ₦5000. Reorder the lines so it prints Change: ₦1400.
questions.explain: The change depends on the total, so the total must be calculated first. Moving total = 1200 * 3; above the change line makes the change 5,000 − 3,600 = 1,400.

questions.q: The delivery fee came from a form as text, so this prints Total: ₦3600500. Fix it so it prints Total: ₦4100. Do not change the line that sets deliveryFee.
questions.explain: Number(deliveryFee) turns the text "500" into the number 500, so + adds instead of gluing. Input from outside must be converted and checked before you use it.

questions.q: Write the processing for an ATM. If the amount is not more than the balance, print New balance: ₦ followed by the new balance. Otherwise print Not enough money. With the inputs given, the program must print Not enough money.
questions.explain: 10,000 is more than 8,000, so the condition amount <= balance is false and the else block runs. With <=, asking for exactly the balance is allowed.

questions.q: Tunde saves ₦4,000 a week towards a ₦30,000 bicycle. Write a loop that adds ₦4,000 at a time until the savings reach the goal, counting the weeks, then print Weeks: 8.
questions.explain: After 7 weeks Tunde has 28,000, which is less than 30,000, so the loop runs once more. After 8 weeks he has 32,000 and the loop stops. Working out "about 7.5, so 8" by hand first tells you the output is right.
